utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. The start of the hearing for today has been delayed for ten minutes due to the Chamber's deliberations on certain matters. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Marije Kamp, who is studying for a master's degree at the University of Utrecht. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Sutherland, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, we left off yesterday discussing the disappearance in July 1992 of Burhanudin Kapetanovic and a person by the surname of Badnjevic. We have evidence in this case - and that's Exhibit P02089 - that Burhanudin Kapetanovic and Asaf Kapetanovic and others were exhumed from a mass grave in Stari Kevljani, a short distance from the Omarska camp. And that's Exhibit P4855 at page 23, and P4853 at pages 28 to 29. Were you aware of them being exhumed from this mass grave?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And regarding the shooting of at least 50 detainees from the village of Hambarine in late July 1992, there is evidence in this case regarding the shooting of dozens of detainees from the Budo [phoen] area in late July. And that's Exhibits P00678, P03478, and P00705. Mr. Gruban, you were also convicted in relation to over 30 other killings and disappearances that occurred on other shifts; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of having been convicted for things that happened in my absence. And as for the killing of 50 people, I claim with full responsibility that that could not have happened. If something of that kind had happened, there are no witnesses from Omarska who wouldn't talk about that event. Imagine if 50 people had been killed, how much shooting should there have been? How many people should have been involved with that? That fact is based on just one witness - I don't want to mention his name because I don't know whether he was protected or not - and in my view that witness didn't tell the truth. There are a lot of arguments which can corroborate my claim that he wasn't telling the truth. I don't know how much time you have. I could go along a long list of facts that would prove that that witness was lying.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, in relation to the killings of detainees directly and personally committed by persons outside of your shift but in furtherance of the described system of ill-treatment and persecution at the camp, in June and July 1992, your trial chamber listed on page 5 and 6 of your judgement, your trial chamber judgement, the names of over 30 people. Now, that's correct, isn't it, that you were found guilty of things that happened and of at least 30 named individuals who were killed or disappeared on other people's shifts, i.e., Mr. Radic or Mr. Kosa's [phoen] shifts. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. Look, Mladic was not the head of shift. I don't know any other Mladic but General Mladic who was not in Omarska at all. Second of all --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I said Mladen -- I said Mr. Radic, meaning Mladjo Radic, Mladen?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, Mladjo Radic. What I heard in the interpretation was Mladic as if Mladic was in Omarska. Let's be very precise. I don't know anything about those 30 persons, and if I wasn't there, I would not speculate on what had happened because many witnesses speculated and that resulted in the position that I'm in. Let's stick to the facts and what I know. I don't know the names of those people. You said that you had names of 30 people. I don't know their names. I don't know who the perpetrators are. I don't know when that happened. Again, we're talking about a mass murder of 30 people, and if that had happened, I would have known or at least I would have heard about that although it was on somebody else's shift.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, these are all individual incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter number 25701, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, you see in front of you the trial chamber first-instance verdict against you, Mejakic, and Dusko Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to page 5, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, we see here the court summarising its findings in relation to you and it says that you -- it mentions the killing of detainees directly -- of persons committed during your shift. And then it mentions the people that were killed outside -- killed or disappeared outside of your shift. Do you see the second paragraph -- the third paragraph under your name?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to page 6 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, you see all these names: Abdulah Puskar and Silvije Saric beaten to death; Emir Ramic, shot and killed; Mehmedalija Sarajlic, beaten to death; Velid Badnjevic, shot and killed; Slavko Ecimovic, beaten to death; Amir Ceric and another man named Avdic, shot and killed; Husein Crnkic sustained injuries to which he eventually succumbed; Jasmin Hrnic, Enver Alic, and Emir Karabasic, beaten to death; Mehmedalija Nasic, shot and killed; Safet Ramadanovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Page 6 of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Safet Ramadanovic, beaten to death. Becir Medunjanin, beaten on multiple occasions and died as a result of beating. Approximately 12 with the surname of Garibovic who were beaten, after which they disappeared without a trace. Dalija Hrnic, beaten to death. Azur Jakupovic, beaten to death and killed along with Edvin Dautovic. Rizah Hadzalic, beaten to death. Miroslav Solaja died as a result of beating. Dr. Osman Mahmuljin, Dr. Eniz Begic, Zijad Mahmuljin, and Ago Sadikovic disappeared from the camp. Esad Mehmedagic disappeared from the camp. Nedzad Seric disappeared. Gordan Kardum, beaten to death. And Emsud Baltic and several men disappeared one evening in July. Then it goes on to describe a killing which resulted from the system of ill-treatment in which you participated in, and that is, in June 1992, Ismet Hodzic died as a result of lack of medication and medical treatment for his diabetes. Now, you remember, do you not, reading in your judgement that you were found guilty of these other crimes as well, of these other murders that occurred or disappearances that occurred in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: I can speak about incidents and individuals that I'm aware of. Now, what happened on other people's shifts, I don't know. I can only give you hearsay evidence and I can't consider myself responsible for something that happened when I was not there. Nowhere in the world is a person found guilty of things that happened on other people's shifts, when he was absent, and things that he didn't agree with. You said Safet Ramadanovic. Safet Ramadanovic died of natural causes in Omarska. His body was handed over to his family; I know that for a fact and I noted that down. Mehmedalija Nasic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the answer be at least as long as the question because the witness has the right to state his opinion of every single name that he heard in the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber discussed this issue yesterday as well. Theoretically the question is whether the witness was convicted for certain matters, so the answer should be either yes or no. But I don't see the point of putting all these things in such a lengthy formulation. It's fair enough for the witness to wish to comment upon those things.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought I asked the question quite simply twice, on two occasions, and then the witness kept evading answering yes or no and so then I went to read out all of the names --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness never challenged his conviction at the Bosnian court, but he said clearly that he did not agree with it. Then you leave it and then proceed. I don't --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- see the point of putting every sentence of the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we proceed?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May I have 65 ter number 10950, please. Now, Your Honour, this is a document that wasn't on my 65 ter list, but subsequent discussions with the Defence and they have no objection to me using it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, this is a "Kozarski Vjesnik" article dated the 9th of April, 1993. It's on -- the paragraph I'm interested in is on page 1 of the English translation, the sixth paragraph, and on page 2 of the B/C/S document on the left-hand side column, the paragraph above the heading at the bottom of the page and it's the -- starts: "More than 6.000 informative talks were held at the gathering centres of 'Omarska,' 'Keraterm,' and 'Trnopolje.' A group of 1.503 Muslims and Croats were taken to the camp of 'Manjaca' with proper documentation proving active participation in conflicts against the Army of the Serb Republic as well as participating in genocide of the Serb people. Instead of receiving their just punishment, the white-world mighty men forced us to release them all from Manjaca." Now, this is an interview with Simo Drljaca, the chief of the SJB, and that was his answer in relation to a question put to him: Recently there has been a lot of controversy about your work and that of the police. How do you judge your work in the past year? And then he said this, what I've just quoted to you. And that reflects, doesn't it, the view that everyone alleged to be involved in conflicts against the Serbs was participating in genocide?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what is your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that that reflects the view that everyone alleged to be involved in conflicts against the Serbs was participating in genocide?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. This -- he's being asked to simply interpret what is written in a newspaper article. If she wants to ask him about what Mr. Drljaca's views were, that's one thing, but this would be complete speculation to just be commenting on some article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't agree. He can -- he can give his opinion as to whether that, in fact, reflects the view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view the witness cannot give his opinion. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, but just to -- I think -- I don't want there to be a misunderstanding. I understand Mr. Robinson to be saying that the question can be posed in a way that asks about what this witness may or may not have known about the views held at the time and about the views held by Drljaca and then -- that's what he was getting at and I think he was trying to direct the examination toward that area. So -- but I fear that Ms. Sutherland may have misunderstood the Court's ruling as a rejection of the inquiry in its entirety and I don't think that was what the Court intended. I think obviously that was not what Mr. Robinson intended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sutherland, can you assist us with the answer you gave to Judge Kwon: "Well, Your Honour, I don't agree. He can give his opinion as to whether that, in fact, reflects the view." This would be his opinion. When you say -- in the strict sense of the word "opinion"?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No. The witness can say whether this -- this was Drljaca's view that he held at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: So this would not be opinion evidence --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: -- as we know it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, anything further on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think my point, Your Honour, was that the Prosecution is asking him to comment on a news article, and then after he makes the comment they're going to -- either to bootstrap it to admit the article either as being consistent or inconsistent with his opinion or his analysis of what Drljaca said. And if we allow that, then every document in the world can somehow become admissible as either consistent or inconsistent with some witness's view. So my point was that what's relevant and probative is what his understanding was of Mr. Drljaca's acts and conduct. Was he somebody who believed that -- or did he -- through his conversations with Drljaca, did he have the understanding that Drljaca thought that anybody who was fighting against the Serbs was committing genocide? But to comment on the news article and to ask the question in that way, in my opinion, is just an effort to bootstrap the admissibility of what otherwise shouldn't be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, if you're going to ask a witness as to the views of somebody else, you really need to establish a basis as to how that might have come about. I mean, did they work together, did they talk together, were they confidants, otherwise it's such a broad question that its probative value is doubtful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue? Are you going to reformulate your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, you were in the reserve police for quite some time, and as a result of that you knew Simo Drljaca, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: I heard about Simo Drljaca and I met him, on the 24th of November, 1992, when the police set out for the theatre of war in Obudovac. He was in charge of that unit. That's when I met him. Before that, while Omarska existed, I heard of his existence but I never communicated with him. I never met him during that period of time. During the existence of Omarska, I didn't report to Drljaca about anything, I did not contact him directly; all that was done through other people. I knew that he was chief, but that was all I knew about him. I didn't have any personal contacts or dealings with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Even if you didn't have personal contacts or dealings with him, were you aware of his attitude towards people that had -- non-Serbs that were alleged to have committed crimes against the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would object to this. I think this is so general and vague: Were you aware of his attitude? I think that she should -- this is eliciting evidence of no probative value whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland, would you like to respond to Mr. Robinson's objection or are you going to reformulate your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'll reformulate my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, people were held in Omarska because they were alleged to have been involved in conflicts against the Serbs and for committing genocide, alleged to have committed genocide against the Serbs; yes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear the word "genocide." However, people in Omarska were kept for having participated in the armed rebellion. That was the first category of those people when the screening was done. And the second category consisted of the people who financed and assisted that rebellion. And the third group were people who were not directly involved in any of that, and the third group of detainees were -- was released and taken to Trnopolje. No trials were conducted against them. The first two groups were transferred to Manjaca and after that I don't know what happened to them, whether they were put on trial or whether they were released under the pressure of the international community as you put it. I really don't know. This is all I know: The third group was released because it was established that they had not participated in the armed conflict. This was the very reason for the existence of the collection centres. People were collected if they were found in the area of combat activities, they were interviewed, they were categorised, and then they were treated accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And people alleged to have been involved in armed rebellion were considered to be involved in genocide; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just told you the word "genocide" has been heard here at this Tribunal and in Sarajevo. Every second person tends to use the word "genocide." Wherever something bad happened, it turns out to be a genocide. I think that this is a bit of an overstatement. It's a big word, "genocide." First of all, you have to be aware of the definition of genocide and then we can use the word with authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. You just said you -- you just said you heard the word here at the Tribunal and in Sarajevo. You mean Sarajevo in Bosnia -- you mean the Bosnian court. Yes, I wanted to clarify because in all your answers you said you didn't hear the word "genocide" at the time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's become a common word now in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in our part of the world. And before the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina there are several persons who stand accused of genocide. Some of them were even found guilty. Now these decisions have been overturned. They were sent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- back to the constitutional court. It was actually the constitutional court that told the court to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When you were in Omarska, did you hear the word "genocide"; that was my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time it was not being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. No basis to tender it through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we have evidence in this case to -- I don't think -- we do have evidence in this case to show that this is the voice of the local authorities, the local Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I don't think we have a basis to admit this through this witness, do we?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, the witness -- the witness is -- has spoken about people being held in Omarska that were allegedly involved in the armed rebellion and the conflicts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will not admit this. Please move on, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, in paragraph 42 of your statement in reference to adjudicated fact 1191, you say that no one was targeted on the basis of their education. And you say that there were testimonies in your trial to the effect that some individuals, physicians, had been taken from the Omarska camp but you don't know for what reason and what happened to them. But it's not just physicians as an occupational group that were targeted, was it, because there were leaders in the community, physicians, politicians, lawyers, businessmen, and police, they were all targeted in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What would you like me to say? What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That it wasn't just physicians who were targeted. It was also politicians, lawyers, police, they were all targeted in Omarska camp. You must know that from -- from even the evidence in your trial.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put this this way: Nobody was targeted according to profession. In my case I heard the testimony of witnesses. I was not present. A lady witness, I'm not going to mention her name, I don't know whether she was protected, she said literally that certain physicians were called out in the middle of the day, 3.00, and were taken out of the camp. So that would be that. As for somebody being particularly targeted due to their profession, I don't think so. You also said lawyers. There were different testimonies in Dr. Stakic's case. It says even in the judgement that a well-known Prijedor lawyer, Ahmet Atarovic, was killed. However, in 2007, reading "Oslobodjenje," a Sarajevo daily newspaper, I found an article stating that Atarovic opened a law office in Prijedor. So that's part of the judgement. Some witness testified - we're not going to mention who it was in order not to reveal that person's identity - saying that such persons were targeted and taken out, not mentioning names, and then later on it turns out that - thank God - these persons are alive and well. And lawyer Tatarevic has an office today both in Sanski Most and Prijedor, and the judgement said what I said. In such cases, quite literally, there is no opposition because when you mention the name of a particular person how can we know where that person is? So believe me, as far as these persons being taken out, as far as that's concerned, there are some people who are still alive and about today. It's hard to go into all of that, but I was not present when these persons were being taken out. There is clear testimony about that. Actually, there weren't any transcripts during my trial so I could not refer to any particular part of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, Mohammed Cehajic, the president of the Municipal Assembly, SDA member, was exhumed in Stari Kevljani. Silvije Saric, the president of the HDZ Prijedor, was exhumed from Kevljani. Becir Medunjanin, the secretary of the People's Defence of Prijedor, exhumed for Kevljani. These are all people that were last seen in Omarska camp. We have -- in relation to the teaching profession, Sadeta Medunjanin, exhumed from Jama Lisac. Abdulah Puskar, a math teacher in secondary school, exhumed from Stari Kevljani. Husein Crnkic, exhumed from Kevljani. Lawyers. We have Esad Mehmedagic exhumed from Stari Kevljani. Nedzad Ceric, the president of the court, exhumed in Stari Kevljani. And then the medical profession. Dr. Esad Sadikovic, exhumed in Hrastova Glavica. Dr. Jusuf Pasic, exhumed in Stari Kevljani. So we do know where these people are, they're dead. And you heard about many of these during your trial. The police. Fikret Sarajlic from Kozarac exhumed in Stari Kevljani. Esad Alic from Kozarac, Stari Kevljani. Mirsad Alic from Kozarac, Jakarina Kosa was where he was exhumed. And I've already mentioned Ago Sadikovic who was exhumed in Stari Kevljani. There's a number of other police that witnesses in this trial have testified to that were last seen in Omarska and were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I refer Your Honours to P02989 at transcript page 19110 to 1921 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's pause here. So what is your question, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban said he didn't know where -- when I said to him that leaders, politicians, businessmen, police, lawyers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the question is --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- were targeted and were, in fact, killed in Omarska --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So does it mean that the people without profession was not targeted?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, I just read quite a number of names to you from different professions, leaders in the community, and it's a fact, isn't it, that those leaders were targeted?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You could have understood from my previous answer that they were not targeted, but let me say this. Sejmenovic Mevludin is also one of the top people who was a member of parliament. It was called the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then Mirza Mujadzic, president of the SDA party for the municipality of Prijedor, he is also a community leader. Thank God these people are still alive. You mentioned the names of quite a few persons here who were exhumed from these graves. I really do not know quite a few of these people that you mentioned. However, for example, you mentioned Dr. Eso Sadikovic, isn't that right? He was taken out of Omarska; that is to say, he was not killed in Omarska, he was taken out with a group of 124 other detainees from Keraterm. It was only he who was added to that group. Later on we found out from the material that I got from you that Dr. Sadikovic was exhumed far away from Omarska, about 150 to 200 kilometres away. So he left Omarska. Unfortunately, he lost his life. Now, how can this be ascribed to somebody who is in Omarska? I don't understand. For example, a person is sent out of Omarska, how can a guard know where this person is going to be taken and what his fate is going to be and so on and so forth. You also mentioned Sadeta, Medunjanin was her last name, the interpretation was not exactly right. I know this is the wife of Becir Medunjanin. She was also taken out in a group and also she was found very far away. I don't know how many kilometres, it must have been more than 150 kilometres away from Omarska. What you said -- well, you spoke at length so I cannot remember exactly now. I cannot record with film precision everything, but certainly people found this those graves were victims of fighting, they were actually casualties from combat, so not all these people are from Omarska. You showed a document yesterday too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, we have evidence in our case, which is P4855 and P4853, which shows a large number of people that were last seen in Omarska having been exhumed. They weren't involved in combat. They were in the camp, they were detained in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, as I understood your last answer, you were saying that these people who were found in graves were casualties from combat.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You misunderstood what I was saying. In these graves there must have been people who were involved in fighting in Kozarac and the surrounding area because yesterday you yourself said that there were casualties on the Muslim side in that fighting. They were buried somewhere. Probably they were buried in these graves too. Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In fact, yesterday it was my position that there was no fighting, that it was in fact shelling by the Serb forces. Okay. We will move on. In paragraph 32 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well -- well, that is your position but it's not realistic, it's not true. Who was it that the Serb army was fighting if there was no one on the other side? We have to be realistic, we have to tell the truth. There was fighting, it went on from the 24th until the 30th, somewhere in the location of Kozarac, and there were clashes there within the Muslim forces themselves. One option was led by the police commander, Didovic who said that war should not be waged, that weapons should be surrendered, that there shouldn't be any combat. There were also extremists who wanted to put up resistance. So there were clashes between them themselves. There was fighting, unfortunately, and once it all happened it was too late.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, there's documentary evidence in this case to say that the fighting -- the -- in Kozarac the mopping-up was occurring on the -- on the 26th of May. It's your evidence that women were not called out and raped or sexually assaulted on your shift and you didn't hear about this happening during other shifts. Even if you didn't know at the time - and I'm not saying that you didn't - you are certainly aware now that many of the women detainees were raped and sexually assaulted by the police guards. You heard this evidence at your trial, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I resolutely deny that as far as I'm concerned. My shift, my stay in Omarska, not a single woman was disturbed in any way by any of the guards from my shift. As a matter of fact, we appointed a guard to be between two rooms where women were put up, so he was there non-stop. Many women witnesses testified. You have the transcripts, and I'm not going to mention her name, she said that she looked forward to see me and that nobody would harass them then and that they could even drink coffee and tea and have a cigarette in our offices when we were on duty. That was their testimony. That is the truth and nothing but the truth, as we say. In the beginning when this Tribunal was being established, when some publicity was supposed to be given to this, there was this centre for training witnesses, where witnesses were being brought. So it was important for somebody to speak up before the public. Again --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I'm going to mention a woman witness, I'm not going to mention her name, she said publicly that she had been raped and then you called her --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, I'm going to interrupt --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please allow me to finish. When you asked her to come and testify here --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, I'm saying to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, let's hear him out. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. This woman witness was called before this court to testify about that rape, and she spoke about that beforehand on television. She received a decoration from Franjo Tudjman and from Boutros Ghali, who was Secretary-General of the UN at the time, because she spoke up; however, that testimony of hers was not true so she refused to testify before this court and therefore did not appear as a witness before this court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, you're aware that women were raped on other shifts other than your shift, aren't you? You heard this evidence in your trial?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: One woman witness said that she was sexually assaulted but not raped. One woman said that she was raped but she didn't know when or how or who raped her or in which shift, and she even tried to say that it was during my shift. And then when the lawyer asked her about that, she apologised and said that it wasn't during my shift. That was that testimony. I'm telling you, I am only speaking about the time when I was present there. During my stay there, I never heard of any such thing happening. Had something like that happened, I would have condemned that, any normal person would. In such moments, even if something like that did actually happen, it should be condemned as such. At that time I had no knowledge whatsoever. Later on I heard during some testimony I told you, these two women appeared before the court and spoke about that; how true it is, you can be the judge of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, said there were no minors in the camp at least under the age of 15. You said that you don't know of a single case of boys younger than 15. We have evidence in this case of a 13-year-old boy whose -- both arms had been freshly broken; and that's at transcript page 20495. You didn't see him being taken into the canteen and being fed by other detainees? You're shaking your head. I take that as a "no."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really did not see something like that. Among these detainees, I did not notice any younger people. There was a group of - how do I put this? - older minors. As soon as it was noticed that they were there, they were released at the very outset. So on the 4th of June, a group was released of 120 people. They were transferred to Trnopolje, these young people. And this group included people who were interrogated at the very beginning and the inspectors had established that they had not participated in the armed rebellion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You say there was no mentally impaired persons in the camp. You're aware of a mentally retarded detainee Asmir Crnalic, nicknamed Vico, being in the camp, are you not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you mispronounced the name. Do you mean the jumping out of the window from the white house, Crnalic Mirsad? Am I right? Take a look. Are we speaking about the same person?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, we are. He was shot, and you actually made inquiries with the detainees on the pista as to his name.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the way it was. Nothing could have been noticed, I mean that the man was ill. During a previous shift he got up, he walked along the piste --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, I'm sorry to interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and he was cursing --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We don't need the details of the incident. I'm simply referring you to the fact that there was a mentally impaired person in the camp. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree, no. It can happen at a particular moment, somebody's behaviour can -- well, you know, you remember the situation in the restaurant, when this man got up and asked others to take part in a rebellion, to rebel. So it's just a moment, but it doesn't mean that that person's mentally impaired. A person can explode at a given moment and then other people try to pacify him, and then you know what happened between him and the guard in the restaurant. This is common knowledge. Witnesses spoke about that, both witnesses for the Prosecution and witnesses for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that there were no physically incapacitated persons in the camp. This is at paragraph 36. Esad Mehmedagic was an almost blind lawyer who worked a public defender who couldn't walk around independently. You don't recall seeing him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know him personally and I never saw any such thing, but I mean it's illogical what the public defender said. Well, in my view, the public defender should be capable person who can read things, see things. I mean, I'm trying to say that I find this illogical. I don't know how you're going to understand what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There were people there that were dependent on insulin therapy, for example, Ismet Hodzic. There were detainees with heart conditions. There were two detainees who suffered from a hearing impairment. There were two deaf mutes. This evidence was led at your trial. Do you still not accept that there were people that were mentally and physically impaired in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for these mentally impaired people, as you call them, I didn't hear of them, I didn't see them. As for this mason from Cerik, he died a natural death. His neighbours said that he was a diabetes patient and he didn't have any medicine. However, let me tell you this: There was a physician, an ambulance, a nurse there, and at first whenever people asked for medical assistance it was provided to them. I mentioned yesterday that there was this major shortage, that the Krajina was cut off from everyone and everything. At home we seemed to have these --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- home pharmacies, if you can call them that. I brought all the medicine I had at home and I gave it to different people, and in court people even got up and thanked me for that. That is what I can say to you. So I am not trying to evade this and say that this man did not die --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but believe me, there is no good detention unit, even in your -- let me finish. In your Detention Unit, too, people have died, so a person can say that that is a lack of medical assistance and so on and so forth, let alone what was happening in Omarska during war and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, please listen to my question. My question was simply: Do you still not accept that there were mentally and physically impaired people in the camp? And that just requires a yes or a no answer.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I do not accept that. I've already said that. Had that happened, somebody would have told me about this, one of my friends or acquaintances who were detained or I would have perceived it visually myself. Even if that happened, then it would have to be reported to the doctor who was at Omarska. I've already said --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, please --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- whenever this kind of situation was established, like in the case of those older minors, these people were released. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 17 you say detainees were allowed access to water, toilets, and could stay outside to wash their face, freshen up and clean the rooms or get their rooms cleaned and that there were showers in the rooms in which the detainees were held. It sounds like a hotel. You state tens of showers and tens of toilets existed in Omarska and were available to detainees. Even counting the number of toilets that you mentioned yesterday, roughly a dozen or even as high as -- even if we put it as high as 20, you do the maths. The number of people that were detained in that camp, you say 2.500, Serb documentation says 3.334, at a minimum, that's about 150 people per toilet, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we could put this on the ELMO and then I can show you where there was water, where there were toilets, and so on. As far as I know, no guards did not allow people access. And you know from my case that people could freely walk about when I was on duty, they could go to the bathroom and so on. Also, when they went up for lunch, one group would finish lunch and then stay on the field next to the white house, and then there was a hose there and people could freshen up. And then there would be a group of people who would clean the room, and then the people were taken back to their rooms. That is the only thing I can say. Also in -- Omarska was not only in that small garage, if you remember at the very beginning, the ground floor of the administration building and water was not in the white house, but detainees could carry water in jerrycans and bottles, take water to these premises, that is. As for all the other premises, there was water, and we, employees, used that water before the war and also those who were detained. This was drinking water, and I think that in the Kvocka case water was analysed and the results were positive, establishing that it was drinking water. There was water that was not drinking water - I've already mentioned this hose - so the people could freshen themselves up. One was in front of the white house and the other was on the eastern side towards the canal where people could wash up and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There was evidence given in the Kvocka trial about -- where guards used the water stream as a weapon making comments like: "Increase the jet, hit the balija, let the jet of water throw them on the ground." Detainees were made to strip naked and wash with the fire hose between the piste and the white house, which is quite a humiliating experience, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I maintain when it was my shift, that hose was used for people to wash up, the jet was mild, and I heard no evidence, no testimony, that somebody misused or abused that hose and turned it into a weapon against the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just getting back to the facilities for personal hygiene. Dr. Slobodan Gajic testified in the Kvocka trial that there were no adequate conditions provided for sleeping, bathing, changing of clothes, personal hygiene in general. And Branko Starcevic from Omarska, he testified at your trial, didn't he? He also gave evidence in the Kvocka trial here. He testified that he was a guard assigned to the hangar building and he said: "There was a stench, a bad smell, and every day I had to wash myself and wash my clothes to wash the smell out." And that's at Kvocka transcript page 9268. So things weren't as rosy as you're putting it, that they were allowed to shower and bathe and the toilet facilities were all working.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, in view of the large number of detainees - and you saw that there was a large number of water facilities, perhaps not enough, but in any case teams of epidemiologists came from Prijedor to chlorinize the toilets to avoid some sort of infection or contagion, but that was two months after the establishment. That group that stayed until the 20th or the 21st of August got proper bedding, proper beds, visits by the International Red Cross, et cetera. Conditions were much better. Of course the rooms were overcrowded. There were more people than should have been per room, but that was the situation and nothing could be changed. You saw on the sketch all the rooms we had, and whenever we could empty a room and make it available to the detainees we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In relation to the food, at paragraph 18 you say that the detainees could eat their meal at their ease and to your knowledge nobody was ill-treated during their meals. Even if there was -- if there was 3.000 detainees and they were sent in groups of 30, even five minutes would take eight hours to feed all of these people, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meals began very early, around 8.00, 9.00, and the distribution of food was not limited. It lasted as long as there was food and as long as there were people who still had to eat. The food perhaps was insufficient and perhaps not of good quality; I described it yesterday. But believe me, for a detainee, there is no good food. Even in your Detention Unit, take the canteen lists for the detainees and you will see that the food is inadequate. Although you have all the conditions that you might desire, whereas we had what we had. Those were young people and, of course, the meals were probably too small for them, but that's the food we had. The guards had the same food just from different tin plates.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, the guards didn't have the same food. The guards, in fact, had better-quality food and the interrogators as well than the detainees. And witnesses testified in your trial that guards were given steak, mashed potato, tomato, and the detainees had a bowl of brothy soup with rotten cabbage and a bit of bread. You, in fact, on one occasion ordered that Senad Kapetanovic be given a meal and he was -- and he was given a meal of steak. Do you recall that evidence in your trial?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do. That was not the food that the guards ate. That was the food that inspectors got, and that happened on a weekend. The inspectors worked for a short while and left and that food was left over. I decided to distribute it to the prisoners and that's how they got that food. As for the guards, the guards really did eat that food. I can show you how the food was distributed and where. Perhaps the guards got larger rations, but it was the same food. The guards of course had the advantage of going home after work and eating better, and I and some other people brought food from home to give to the detainees, but you probably know that. You know the whole case file.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been advised that my time is up. I would seek your indulgence for another 10 to 15 minutes, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I wish to play a short video-clip. This is 65 ter number 40424D, and the time code I wish to play is from 20.43 to 23.26, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, this is a video taken by the foreign journalists when they visited the camp on the 5th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gruban, that doesn't look like people eating at their leisure, does it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't see anybody forcing them to eat up and finish so quickly. I just see people appearing and then eating, then leaving, and the next group coming. Do you -- did you see anyone forcing them to hurry-up? I did not see it in this recording.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 18 that meals were distributed in the camp under the supervision of two chefs. These two chefs, as you call them, didn't cook the meals. They were done in the Separacija building which, as you said yesterday, was 1 and a half kilometres away; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I described yesterday where the food was prepared and there were two cooks there just to supervise. The food was distributed by the detainees. You could see it in this video. There was one of them I remember called Ago who handed out food, and these detainees, women, helped with the washing of dishes. They volunteered for their work --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because they found the day was too long and they had nothing to do so they offered to wash dishes, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You know Cedo Voluta -- Cedo Vuleta?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe Cedo Vuleta. Veleta does not exist as a name where I live.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He was a mine worker who worked in the electrical shop in the hangar building. You know who I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I know Cedo Vuleta. He was an electrician and he still is an electrician.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, he said that detainees -- some guards would slap and kick detainees when they went to eat, and this happened on your shift, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard anything like that, nor did anyone claim that during my trial. You know yourself that when it was my shift, all the witnesses said nobody mistreated them and they could eat in peace. This Cedo Vuleta was an electrician working on maintenance, and at that time there was a group of mine workers who were in charge of cleaning and maintenance --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and he had no contact whatsoever with detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, he testified in the Kvocka case at transcript page 7474 to 7475 that some guards on your shift would slap and kick the detainees when they went to eat, even when you told them not to.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any such thing and I don't know how he came up with that. Excuse me, did he mention a particular guard by name, so we can look into it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, you said that in some cases -- there was some cases of individual armed groups coming to the camp and ill-treating the detainees. Specifically who are you referring to when you said these individual armed groups?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, there were no major cases of that kind, but I heard that some people came when I was absent and those were renegade paramilitaries who did not belong to the Territorial Defence or the army or the police. They were simply armed men who came to settle some accounts from the past with certain people. That's how they barged in --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- well-armed --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that persons in the police or the military could enter the camp at any time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an external ring kept by the Territorial Defence from Omarska and those were people --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, I'm sorry to --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of diminished capacity and --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. My question was simply: Persons in the police or the military could enter the camp and come into the Omarska compound where the detainees were being kept; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Early on they could. However, later passes were created and there was a gate away from Omarska centre. There were two people from the Territorial Defence, a receptionist, and two guards from Omarska, and they did their best to stop people without passes from getting in. However, not the entire complex was fenced in, so you could get in from several directions. And the Territorial Defence that was supposed to prevent unauthorised entry did not do their job, so it was possible to get in. These people could get into Omarska. However, efforts were made to stop them. There were cases when they were stopped, disarmed, turned over to the military police if they were in uniform or to the civilian police if they were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, shall we continue after a break?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break of -- for 40 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and may I tender the video-clip, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6686, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are not tendering the transcript of that video?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just the video?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It was basically -- we have that footage under another exhibit, I think, parts of that footage, but it was basically for the visual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. When we resume, how much more would you need, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ten minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at ten past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, in paragraph 41 of your statement in relation to adjudicated fact 1190 concerning the large number of bodies frequently seen in the grounds of the detention camp, there's evidence in this case that dead bodies were seen on a daily basis. Now, is it your evidence that even though you worked at the camp for almost three months, you never saw a single dead body in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see some dead bodies, but certainly not the way it's described here. Those were isolated cases, not large heaps of bodies as is stated here. I did see some bodies, individual bodies, we can discuss that, but a large number on a daily basis, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Whereabouts did you see these bodies that you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for instance, that man who jumped out of the window, his body was on the ground on the southern side of the white house. Then the man Alija Nasic who got killed in the restaurant, his body was found by the collector for filtering wastewater.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Besides these two persons, did you ever see any other bodies in the camp, dead bodies in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the body of Safet Ramadanovic who died in that room that we saw yesterday, A9. The body was taken out. I saw the body of -- I can't remember the first name, Ganic is the last name, he also died in the same room. His body was removed. I know for a fact that these two bodies were given to the families and buried at the local cemetery in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And again, besides people that died of natural causes, did you see any other dead bodies in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's mostly those that I just listed, but what I saw and what I heard are two different things. Before my arrival, when the first prisoners were brought, there was some shooting, and I believe two or three detainees were killed, I was not a witness but I heard that two or three men tried to escape --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- from the group of detainees and they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The Court has heard evidence about that incident. You've heard about the Tomasica site as a burial pit for Muslims who had been killed; yes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that in the last month or two from the media. Before that, I didn't have any information about that. I just heard on TV recently that there are some bodies there, and I don't think there are any bodies from Omarska there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So you didn't ever --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You didn't ever go to the Tomasica mine area where the mass grave is that is being exhumed now, you didn't ever go there after the establishment of the Omarska camp? You shook your head. I take that as a "no"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly didn't and I don't know to this day where this location is. The area of Tomasica is rather large, the mine is also a big complex. I don't know the exact location to this day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, you know about the room 3 massacre at the Keraterm camp that occurred on or about the 24th of July, 1992. Did you ever go to the burial site where the victims of the room 3 massacre were taken?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. I only heard about it through witness evidence. I've never been in Keraterm. I heard, just like you did, that this incident happened, but what really happened I cannot say, it would be just speculation because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you didn't go to the burial site of the victims from this massacre?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, really. To date I do not know where the site is. Maybe local cemeteries in that area, probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you ever interviewed by any RS MUP officials in relation to investigating you or other personnel who worked at the Omarska camp about crimes that had been committed against the non-Serbs in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that anybody talked to me from the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Not from -- not from the headquarters or not from CSB Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: After you left the camp on the 21st of August, 1992, you continued as a reserve policeman, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you were in a police battalion which was established, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the reserve policemen work or place themselves at the disposal of the SJB, so they do all the tasks that they're asked to. Reserve policemen cannot independently carry on internal affairs duties because they are not trained and they need to be accompanied by an active-duty trained policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said earlier today at transcript page 10 that in November 1992 you went to a place called Obudovac, that's how it's in the transcript. I may be mispronouncing the location you went to.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The police battalion from Prijedor went there. I was its member as a reserve policeman. We went to that theatre of war. We spent approximately a fortnight there and then we returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you were in one of the seven companies that were part of this battalion; no?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know how many companies there were, but indeed I was a member of one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And did you go to the front lines at Orasje?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, it was Obudovac. The exact location was Obudovac. We were deployed along that road. We were on duty there for some 15 days. There was no fighting to speak of. Two of our members got killed and a dozen or so were wounded. Basically we were manning that line.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In February 1993, did you go to the front lines at Orasje?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, no. That was the only theatre of war where I was in that area. I was in Obudovac in November 1992. In the morning on the 24th we set out. I know that for a fact because it's my biggest religious holiday and that's when we were deployed to that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, finally I just want to show you one -- two -- two sketches.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 26000, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You brought along some documents which were exhibited as D04313, and you hand-drew the first floor and the ground floor of the hangar building, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drew a plan of the first floor, and then from your team - and I don't know whether you were with that team at the time - I received a ground-floor plan. Now, what we have on the screen now is a plan of that workshop which was on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- later on -- I apologise. And later on I realised that you also have a similar plan of the first floor; however, I didn't have it at the time. I only had what I just told you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to show you that. And if we can go to -- so this is the -- the first page is the ground floor, and if we can go to the second page, we see the same diagram but it has the measurements on it. And it's got the scale for the -- the measurements for the rooms. And if we go to the following page we see -- this is the layout of the first floor and that's what you were talking about a moment ago when you said that --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- that this was available, which -- and so this diagram actually shows pages 4 and 5 of your Exhibit D04313, where you've drawn it on two pages. This is, in fact, the proper layout as it is at the Omarska mine, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we can go to the following page, that, then, also has the dimensions of each of the rooms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this and I can say from the bar table that these diagrams as well as the ones for the administration building were compiled by the OTP from plans that were seized from the Ljubija iron ore mine in February 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6687, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this plan different from what we received yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first two pages, the ground-floor plan, is the same as --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, the first page of that exhibit. It's just that -- I'd simply had it all uploaded under the one number, but then this page 4 and page 5 which are Mr. Gruban's hand-drawn -- hand-drawings, that is actually the first floor which is now page 3 in this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour, and I thank you very much for your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, please, if you will allow me. Is there a difference perhaps, according to you, in what I drew up and what you have shown me? Let's clarify things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I stand -- I stand by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If necessary, Mr. Karadzic will ask you about that. Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can clarify things on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gruban, do you agree with the dimensions of these rooms?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get P87 back on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it would be useful to compare the two and see whether there are any differences. Even if you display it, I will find it difficult to provide any comments because --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I gave the Registrar a wrong number. It should be P6687. We had it on the screen just a minute ago. Can we start with page 1 or is this the whole of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can see the ERN number, Mr. Gruban. Could you please tell us whether you agree -- oh, there are no dimensions here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise. This is the ground floor. What can you tell us about the ground floor?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already told you and I have already made changes to the document that was on the screen yesterday, and I stand by it. I suppose that you will go to the site. You can check and I state that my remarks are reliable. There are no aberrations to what I said because I had spent five or six years working in this company. I would change in this workshop and I am sure that I really know it very well and that I could not have made a mistake. I don't know what objections could anybody have to what I drew up. If there are any objections, I'd like to hear them right away. If there is anything that is not correct, then I'd like to hear it. If everything's correct, why waste time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In front of me I have your drawing of the ground floor. This is the third page of the document that was admitted yesterday --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the document number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Everything is identical. Only the ERN number is missing. Everything is the same, even the mistakes are the same.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And here it says ground floor again. How does this differ from the previous page? Here we can also see dimensions; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The page is the same only the -- the dimensions were added. Do you agree with these dimensions, 5 metres, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I can't see the figures well. However, if we compare them with my own and if they're correct, of course I'll agree. Maybe the Prosecutor could help us. Do they see a difference? If you see a difference, please go ahead and tell me. Feel free.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with these diagrams? Did you check your own drawings against this drawing?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only if the figures match my own, then I can agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And does this apply to all the levels?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to avoid any confusion, just a moment ago you were asked about your deployment in the theatre of war. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber about the positions of Orasje and Obudovac. What is their position vis-à-vis the corridor?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obudovac is on the road from Banja Luka to Brcko. On the left-hand side there is a curve and the road forks off towards Obudovac and it's just before Brcko. And Orasje, on the other hand, is on the Croatian side, on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But not far away?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether there is a river there. In any case, Obudovac is on the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the decision of the Bosnian court it says that you were involved in illegal incarcerations or unlawful detentions. Who was it who arrested and detained prisoners in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: None of the police officers in Omarska including myself brought people to Omarska. One group were captured by the army on Mount Kozara. There were all sorts of arrests on reports, on official notes. For example, somebody reported to the police station a person who allegedly hid weapons in the apartment or participated in an attack, then the police would be sent to inspect. And if they found anything suspicious, they would bring people in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the judgement that was read out to you it says that all those were unlawful arrests without any grounds. We'll come back to that. Madam Sutherland earlier today said that there was no fighting going on, but rather that there was a unilateral attack on Muslim civilian areas. You denied that. But I would like to show you a document now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D26633.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you stand by your claim that this is not correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your question, what is not correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That it is not correct that there were only attacks on various settlements without an actual conflict?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the document which was issued on the 30th of May, 1992, and what does it talk about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was issued by the public security station in Prijedor. It is a dispatch -- actually, it is an official note which was sent to the security services centre in Banja Luka. It says: "Please be informed that in the fighting in the town of Prijedor on the 30th of May, 1992, according to the information at our disposal, we suffered the following casualties. "Killed ..." And then there is a list of names. In any case, there were a total of seven casualties, of whom three were killed and four were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It happened in the course of just one day. How would you assess the casualties suffered by the civilian police in the course of one day?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day 17 police officers and soldiers were killed. In any case, they were killed during that attack that happened on the 30th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D4414, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I'd like to call up 1D25950.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd of June, Drljaca reported that that there were eight wounded. How does this correspond with what you know and what you experienced?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there were wounded at the time. I even know some of those people who were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Miroslav Niksic. He is -- still works at the Tomasica mine. He was my neighbour from a neighbouring village and he's still disabled to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D4415, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we saw a telegram sent by the state security. The document was admitted under a P number. It says that on the 28th of May, before the attack on Prijedor, there were five killed, a dozen wounded on our side, and that from several reliable sources the enemy losses could be estimated to several hundreds. Do you know where the few hundred people who were killed were buried?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know where they were buried. I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly. I suppose they were buried in those villages where people got killed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document I'm talking about is P6685 and it was admitted into evidence yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here and in the judgement rendered by the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina that people were detained without any reason whatsoever and that it was done arbitrarily or people held in high esteem were selected. Can you tell us briefly about the procedure that was followed when somebody ended up in the investigation centre. What happened? Were they kept there just for no reason at all or did they undergo a certain proceeding?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When a person was detained in a collection centre, they would be accommodated in one of the rooms and they are prevented from meeting anybody whom they could influence. And then the person is interviewed, a statement is taken from them. That statement is typed, as I told you. And then the heads of inspector teams make their assessment on the involvement. I spoke about those three categories. There was this category that was released, allowed to go home. At first they were releases. I said in the beginning there were 120 persons and then they were released immediately after the investigation was over. However, later the release stopped, as far as I was informed, because some persons would be released and then there were complaints that they took part in some other hostile activities, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D88315. 1D8815.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was in charge? Who basically carried out these pre-trial proceedings and are you aware of this? What is all of this about? We haven't got a translation yet.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an official note that was written up after an interview with a particular person - we're not going to refer to that person's name, we shouldn't make it public, and this person is from a particular village - and then there is a brief description as to what this person stated, what this person participated in and so on and so forth. And finally, this was not signed but it does say down here "authorised official." At any rate, this is the type of document that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The 23rd of June, that's when this arrived.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When was this person questioned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 30th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please take a look at this, this second paragraph, the end. It says here: "In a shelter with several families on the 29th of May ..." And then in the third paragraph he says where he bought weapons. Can you read out the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "These positions" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the one down here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
