utterances.text: "Some people wanted to hand over weapons, but they didn't dare to because of others." This is exactly what I told you about today. There were several factions, if you will. There were some who were aware of the situation, that they could not cut off the road, that they were surrounded, that it would be a good idea for them to hand over their weapons so that there wouldn't be a conflict, fighting, and so on. However, there were people who thought different. Unfortunately, there was an armed conflict in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be marked for identification so that we don't go on looking through it. This is investigation material of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness hasn't -- hasn't been able to speak to, um, either of these documents in relation to, um, the people that were either arrested.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond? I believe that the witness did confirm not only the content but, what I find even more important, the type of document that was being produced immediately after an arrest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just explain? These inspectors are from three security branches: Public security, state security, military security. They interviewed persons, they took statements, they were handwritten. In this office where I was - I spoke about that yesterday - there were two typists, two women typists, who typed these statements up. They used those mechanical typewriters, computers didn't exist at that time. This kind of typewritten statement was returned then, and then the person was asked to come in again and sign the typewritten statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this is an official note, the essence of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were these people detained in Omarska at the time, Mr. Gruban?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How do we know that they were Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, every day interrogations took place; that is to say, whoever came to Omarska was interrogated, interviewed. A statement would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- taken from such a person and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is whether we can find the passage referring to Omarska in this document? Because we can't read it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the previous page, please. The last sentence in the first paragraph, and up here we see the number 11-12-02-2, so it's not the station, it's another investigation centre, Omarska. I believe that that can be seen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and the -- and is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't understand the end of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're just simply leading the witness. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that was my point, that was Mr. Karadzic saying that. We have no evidence whatsoever in this case that 11-12-02-2 is Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Gruban, can we find the passage that tells us that this document refers to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, here this sentence that I started reading out, at the end --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- at the end it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- read it very slow so that the interpreters can interpret. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we please be told where this sentence is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just read the last sentence, then, so that we don't waste any time. So: He and his wife surrendered when there was this call to surrender, together with women, old men, and children on the 29th of May, 1992, and they were sent to Lamovita and from Lamovita to Omarska. So that is to say to Lamovita first and then to Omarska. So there is no other place in Omarska but for this collection centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark for identification first two pages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, on page 5 as well it says: Is in the collection centre of Omarska. Page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You didn't use it. We'll mark it for -- we'll mark first two pages for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D4416, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm going to bar table that, then. 1D9647, could that be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's the same topic. Could you just take a look at the document and tell us whether it is the same type of document. And also the fourth line from the top of the page, does it say that they were staying in Omarska? Do you find these names familiar, I mean the names he mentions, Cirkin?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Cirkin, I heard of him. He was commander of the defence in the area of Kozarac. Otherwise, he's a captain. That was his profession in the former JNA. He left the former JNA as such. Let me see, Besim Alic, I heard of this Becir. So I know that. The date is the 6th of June, 1992. It's an official note that was drawn up on the 30th of May, 1992, and based on an interview conducted with and then there is a name referred to here - I shouldn't refer to names, should I? - and then the following statement is provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please just speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Over here, Jakupovic, down there, it says intervention platoons were formed made of special unit members and in each of the 30 companies there were 20 special units members, they had better weapons, et cetera. The special units members in my company were Suljo Kusuran, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of Suljo Kusuran, he was one of the leaders in Kozarac as well. I don't know what rank he held, but he was often mentioned, Suljo Kusuran, as one of the leading people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, such a statement made by one detainee, was that sufficient for bringing in those that he mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, precisely. After one interview when a person would mention other persons in his statement, then a signal would be sent out automatically to bring in those other persons and to have them interviewed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this please be admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, may I just add something? You see the last sentence here? Very often it would happen that some persons would be asked to come in for interviews several times. The policeman says at the end, he presents his opinion: "I believe that it is necessary to continue interviewing" this person, this person who provided that statement, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, again we have no evidence from the witness that he knows that -- anything about this person and whether they were in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, were these people in Omarska or this individual, Jakupovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, it's hard for me to remember each and every person individually. Now, there were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- some persons who were there and there were others --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, my question is: Can you know through this document, based on this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of this document one could conclude that this person was in Omarska and was interviewed in Omarska. As for the exact name, I cannot confirm that because I really do not recall. I mean, it's been a long time and there were many people and I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please, let's deal with this one by one. How can you conclude that this individual was in Omarska on the basis of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely because this is how these interviews were conducted, and in this way these official notes were drawn up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Interviews were conducted in various SJBs, not only in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but all the persons who were detained in Omarska were interviewed in Omarska, that is to say, upstairs in that administration building that we spoke about. It was in this single office where the inspection teams were, 30 or 40 persons, I think that they came every day except for weekends, and they conducted these interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it, but I'm not sure if the Prosecution is challenging that some investigation or interviews were conducted. Do you contend that interviews were investigations were taking place at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, we don't dispute that, Your Honour, but it's our case that people were just rounded up and brought in en masse without any justification for their detention whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you do not challenge there was some investigations or interviews?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And there's been evidence to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4417, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please keep this for a minute. Could we please have the document returned in view of what Ms. Sutherland said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, the composition of the staff is mentioned here, Cirkin Alic, Paratusic, and Becir Medunjanin. What was the function of Becir Medunjanin, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, he worked in the people's defence department in Prijedor after the multi-party elections, after these multi-party elections were held in Prijedor. So the portfolio he had was National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And he took an oath to which state? Which army? Which ministry?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the very beginning when the authorities were still functioning, it was the JNA; but afterwards there was stratification. The Muslims set up their own army and he was one of the main persons in charge in that army of theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your view, was he brought in because he is Becir, a Muslim, because he's prominent? Or were there grounds for bringing him in?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was brought in because he was the main activist in the area of Kozarac. He, Captain Cirkin, and many others whom I cannot remember now but we talked about that Kusuran, others. There are quite a few of them. It's been many years and I really cannot remember all of these guys, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to insist on this any longer then. Or rather, I'm not going to show any more documents. Mr. Gruban, in your opinion, a moment ago you said that and also you said that there were three different outcomes. Why were such documents compiled, these interviews, what was the point?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interviews were conducted precisely for that reason, to see which persons were involved in combat and which persons were not. And indeed, when it was established that some persons were not involved, they were released, they were allowed to go home, they were in Trnopolje, they were allowed to go home. So that is this third category that we talked about, third category of persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D -- actually, 4645. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at this, please. It's the 1st of June and the act was committed on the 25th of May. Can you tell us something, for how long is this person detained?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For three days. So the usual police custody, three days. After that, an investigating judge must issue a decision to extend remand. The police is allowed to keep a person in detention, in remand, for 72 hours and it must be an authorised officer of internal affairs. After that, the person is placed under the jurisdiction of an investigating judge who decides what measures, if any, to apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you look at the statement of reasons, what is the charge? Of what is this person suspected?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Remand in prison is ordered under Article 196, paragraph 2, of the criminal code because there is a danger of flight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But look at the statement of reasons. On the 22nd of May, he's suspected of having shot, having fired at and killed five soldiers together with certain persons.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with Mirza Mujadzic, Emir Mujadzic, Esef Crnkic -- oh, I'm sorry, I'm speaking too fast. Do you want me to repeat? The names. Together with Mirza Mujadzic, Emir Mujadzic, Esef Crnkic, and other persons, he committed an armed attack on a Golf vehicle, inside which there were five soldiers and one civilian, killing two soldiers on the spot and seriously injuring two other soldiers, one of whom died subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an incident that happened in Hambarine on the 22nd of May, when fire was opened at this Volkswagen Golf vehicle, killing two soldiers, one other was wounded, a man called Milojica, and I watched that on our local TV Banja Luka. There is evidence in this case. Even Aziz Aliskovic was mentioned as having possibly participated in this as well as another man called Sikiric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was on the 22nd, so before the major attack and the detention of many people. After the attack, was it possible to observe the usual procedure of 72 hours' detention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm not sure where we are heading. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that Mr. Karadzic refrain from leading the witness and using the witness as a conduit to just read documents into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please use your time efficiently.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise. Can this be admitted for identification? The problem is there is no translation. If we had a translation, I'll go -- I would go through it very fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that it uses the same document number, we will mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D4418, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D4610 is the next document I would like to show the witness to see the outcome of this police work and investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you not put your question before putting the document to the witness? Let's collapse it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Excellencies, a moment ago the witness mentioned three categories, those whose guilt was established, criminal charges were filed against them. I want to show the path, to show the exact procedure. Detention, first interview, decision in the investigation, and criminal report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Gruban was a reserve policeman, nothing else. He -- he wasn't involved in any of this, and I don't see how Mr. Karadzic can be putting these documents in through Mr. Gruban.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond? The Prosecution suggested and put it to Gruban, including the judgement from the Bosnian court, that people were arrested and detained because they were prominent or arrested randomly. But there is evidence it was not so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You stated that it was the Prosecution's case that people were just rounded up and brought in en masse without any justification for their detention and whatsoever. So before putting the question, you can ask him whether there were criminal proceedings that followed with respect to the detainees in Omarska, without putting the -- before putting the document, whether he knows or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He already answered about the three categories but I'll ask again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, what followed after the first interviews? What kind of resolution was found in these cases?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said the third category was released to go home. The first and second categories were transferred to Manjaca. Whether there was some prosecution against them, I don't know, but I know that some investigating judges came to Omarska and somewhere among the papers I received from the Prosecution, from the OTP, I did see some criminal reports that had been filed against a number of persons, although not many. I got that from the OTP, they have this, and that is widely known. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I show two documents now, criminal reports?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First, when putting the document, first establish that the document is related to the detainees in Omarska. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I get 1D26644.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, do you know whether these persons had been detained and interrogated in Omarska, Sejad Cirkin, Suljo Kusuran, et cetera, I won't read all the names. And on the second page there is an indication that some of them are at large, are fugitives, some are in detention and some are fugitives. Where were they detained, do you remember? Where was this processing done?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly where they were detained, in which room. You see there are quite a few people here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember Saban Poljak, detained; Zijad Jakupovic, detained, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember a lot of people with the last name Jakupovic and Poljak, but it was a long time ago. It's too hard to remember, and I don't want to get the names wrong. I know there were a lot of people called Poljak and Jakupovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On what basis is a criminal report filed and to whom?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A criminal report is filed based on evidence gathered during investigating actions, that is shown to the investigating judge, and he decides whether there are enough elements to start proceedings or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness hasn't been able to give any evidence in relation to these people listed on -- in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If we see the last page, it refers to the official note that we have already admitted, for example, Sabahudin Jakupovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I can't see the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, last page. Which is one of the supporting evidence, allegedly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4419, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D26634, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are these names familiar? Was any one of them detained in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this document's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, these names are familiar. Some of them. For instance, number 1, yes. Number 2 was not detained, he escaped when all these events started and together with a group of people he broke out towards Cazin Krajina. Person number 3 was not detained. Number 5, yes. That's what I can remember to begin with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you know the exhibit number, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'll just ask Mr. Reid to find it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I suppose it's not ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4420, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's part of D4528.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think we reached that number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we establish that, maybe we'll save one number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At page 29 of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A different ERN number, I have a different number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the text is the same of the one and the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said after the criminal report what follows and who makes that next step?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I am the witness who can deal with this properly, but after this comes prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 1D4610.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you just confirm the date, this was on the 3rd of June; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has just said that he's not the witness who can properly deal with these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With respect to matters that followed this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So let's see whether the witness can confirm anything with respect to this document, 1D4610.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is this step taken on the 5th of June, 1992, two days after the criminal report?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the heading we see lower court in Prijedor, 5 June 1992, and it says investigating judge of the lower court in Prijedor followed by a name --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Karadzic, when you uploaded this document a moment ago I asked you to establish first if this is related to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, we can ask the witness. He already confirmed that these people had been detained in Omarska. I mean, some were fugitives but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- some were detained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't remember that, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, I can answer. For instance, person number 3 was detained, number 4 was detained. I know about them for sure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please, in both versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, continue, Mr. Karadzic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On this page do you see names of people who were there, Kaltak, Sikiric, Popovac?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, person number 10, number 11, number 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's possible this document is already in evidence as part of a larger document. I only wanted to see -- so between the 1st and 5 June, an investigation already started. When was Omarska established as a collection centre?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 31st of May. We have a document that describes the establishment of the collection centre of Omarska in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just look at one more document on the subject, 1D25947.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many people were prosecuted and how many people were released to go home, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a document that says an independent commission of the CSB Banja Luka toured Prijedor and made a report - you probably have that report - and the report says that 1700 approximately were released from -- released to go home, whereas 1300 were forwarded to Manjaca for investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So more than 50 per cent were released?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I also mentioned the smaller groups that were released in early days, 120 people, for instance, in the first group and some other people were later detained, about 120 of them, people who said they had health problems, et cetera, or special needs. And the policemen transported people in their little minibus. Those were some details that I didn't know about but I heard about it during the trial. There was one person who was driven away home by the inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about these people, Alagic, Dokmadjic [phoen], this is a criminal report, the date is 22nd June. Were these people also detained there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 4, yes; number 5 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page in Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the English translation isn't -- the English -- right English translation for the document that's in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's one of the pages. In Serbian it's number 1840, that's seven pages further. The translation only lists people who attacked. The translation has to be completed. Could you please show page 1840, that's seven pages further. This is one part of the document but it seems that only the rest of it has been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the list and tell us whether some of them or all of them were detained.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, number 1, number 2, number 3. I'm sure about those. I believe that there were others, but it was a long time ago so it's impossible to remember every single individual. I'm sure about 21, 23 as well, 17, I even read his statement he witnessed in some cases. But after such a long time I really can't remember every single name, every single individual with certainty. I remember some and I am telling you only about those for whom I am a hundred per cent sure that they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the whole document be admitted and marked for identification because its first half has not been translated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- I'd like to reserve the right to comment on this once I can actually see the whole document once it's been translated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the purpose of marking it for identification, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be MFI D4420, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you tender the 1D4610 or was it part of the already-existing exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's just a part, then it doesn't have to be admitted; but if you find it easier, perhaps it can be admitted under a separate number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's for you to indicate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's a part, then we don't have to tender it. We have established that it is a part of a larger document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When they were arrested and captured were some pieces of evidence seized, documents or weapons, and could any of those be used as the grounds of future processing?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course people did surrender weapons and those were those photographed and even shown on local TV. And from the prosecutor team in my case I received lists aggregated by platoons and companies and squads which were deployed in the area at the time. I don't know how they obtained that information, where their documents were seized, but that's what I received from them. I don't know whether that happened when they ransacked the public security station. In any case, I saw those things.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up 1D25900. Your Excellencies, I will need perhaps three or four more minutes or perhaps five after the break time. So I would kindly ask you to grant me that time in order to complete this witness's testimony. [In English] Maybe it was not clear. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You want to take a break now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No, sir, no. I would like to finish before the break, so I think we can -- we can finish everything before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, there are also several matters after we finish this witness's evidence, but please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay. Then I will tender only these and two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now can you tell us, from the 20th of August -- it seems that there is no translation. Read the first passage. What does it speak about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to a dispatch number and the date, we inform you that in the territory of Prijedor municipality no documents were confiscated that would indicate that the Republic of Croatia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and its armed forces participated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How is this related to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second paragraph says that the confiscated documents point to the fact that Muslim and Croatian people organised themselves in the territory of the municipality in order to mount a fierce attack and a show-down against the Serbs, and that was the grounds for the interrogations and detentions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, now that Mr. Karadzic has read the whole document into the record -- I mean, this witness hasn't comment -- hasn't commented on it and is in no position to comment on the contents of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And document numbers referred to in this document are different from the one we saw earlier on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If not the witness, I can say that this was a dispatch sent from the public security station. This is not part of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So how is this related to Omarska? Establish with the witness first. You are not giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the witness whether when people were arrested and brought in, some materials were found which presented a grounds for their detention in Omarska, and that is a question that I put before I called up the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and the witness said "yes." And in addition to weapons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where does this document -- in this document we can find the passage to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, Omarska is not mentioned but the detainees are and what was confiscated during their arrests, and those who were arrested were sent either to Omarska or Keraterm. There was no third place of that kind where they could be sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban, does it say that it refers to the detainees in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the last paragraph of this official note, chief probably had more information than I did because I was not privy to any of that. However, it seems that during the investigation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gruban --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- he obtained information about all those things and found it necessary to inform about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic's time is very precious. Do you know this or not? You don't know whether this is related to detainees in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really did not have such a document in my hands and I suppose that the person who signed it had it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure you should have -- you should deal with this document after having submitted all those documents --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's up to you. But I don't think we have a basis to admit this one through this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked and you answered about groups who were involved in the commission of crimes. Were there groups who committed crimes and what was the attitude of legal authorities towards that phenomenon and towards those groups?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already spoken about that and I've said that attempts were made to prevent such groups in their dealings. Sometimes it was successful and sometimes it wasn't. And the goodwill existed and as much as possible things were done with the available forces.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up 1D26637. Thank you. I'm interested in the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the last page we can see the code-name for state security, or rather, for that group used by the state security. In conclusion it says that: "Only a strong and legal government based on democratic and rational principles, to say nothing of humane principles, can guarantee the prospects and the future of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." This is a recommendation by the state security. How does this tally with your experience of the position of the official authorities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course only a strong government can maintain peace and order through legal institutions such as the MUP, the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we have the previous page in Serbian and the English page can remain as it is. [In English] "We are under the impression ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says: "We are under the impression that the regular units and commanding officers of the Army of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina are impotent to deal with these individuals and informal groups which are fighting on the side of the Serbian people for their own sake and profit ..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then can we see the following page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says: "There is the serious danger that extremist individuals from our side may seize power and thus prevent the legal establishment of government." Would you say that this is an exaggeration? How do you see this? And how does this tally with what you know about the position of the authorities in Republika Srpska and in Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time during war time when everybody was armed, what surfaces is everybody's ego, and you can actually tell about people and what they're like. There were individuals and groups who wanted to achieve material gain and they committed crimes. The military was there, the police was there because they were afraid of them. In every war and in every single area there are cases like that. Sometimes there were successes in preventing those groups; sometimes it was impossible. In 1992, the police station in Omarska was taken over by a military formation, or rather, a paramilitary formation - I don't know what to call it. A legal police station was taken over and that paramilitary group held it for some 20 days or so. And later on the situation was reinstated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that this was on the 29th of May, one day before the attack on Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GRUBAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the left-hand side corner it says 165/92 [as interpreted] which means it was sent on the 29th.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, can this be admitted and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4421, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: If you don't have more than one issue, we probably could have finished right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Gruban, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wish you a lot of success in your work and thank you for granting me this provisional release.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I don't know whether I was clear. If the only matter is discussion about my testimony, we can finish it before the break and save some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We understood that way. Before that, Mr. Tieger, yesterday the accused filed the bar table motion related General Miletic's document. The motion contains references to the fact that you do not object to the admission of the document. However, the Chamber wanted to check whether you are minded to file a further response.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That communication did not come directly through me, so -- and I understood initially that we were working on a response. Perhaps I can provide the Court with an answer either before we adjourn or immediately after by e-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. The Chamber conveyed the wish to hear in relation to the communications between the accused and his legal adviser during the course of his testimony to the parties through the Legal Officer of the Chamber. So shall we hear from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, we take the position that there ought to be no restrictions on the communications between Dr. Karadzic and myself during his testimony, and we base that on the Prlic Appeals Chamber's decision on the Prosecution's appeal against the Trial Chamber's order on contact between the accused and counsel during an accused's testimony pursuant to Rule 85(C), which was decided on the 5th of September, 2008. And in that decision, the Appeals Chamber held that the general prohibition of contact between a witness and the parties doesn't prohibit, per se, communications between the accused and his counsel when he's a witness. And they went on to find that the order of the Chamber in Prlic was correct or proper within its discretion in not prohibiting contact between the accused and his counsel. So that was later followed by another Trial Chamber order in the Prlic case when the issue came up again in the course of cross-examination, and whether once the documents were disclosed that were to be used in cross-examination the -- there ought to be some restriction on contact. And the Prlic Chamber said no, and that was in an order of the 11th of June, 2009, clarifying the relationship between counsel and an accused testifying within the meaning of Rule 85(C). So it's our position that the jurisprudence is clear that there need be no restriction between counsel and the accused when the accused is giving testimony. It's a little bit different in this case because he is self-represented and I'm his legal adviser, but you have essentially imposed me as his counsel for the purpose of questioning him during his examination and I don't think that difference then would change the outcome. So that's our submission on this issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To be allowed to contact is one thing, and then to what extent they can communicate is another thing. So could you -- do you have any observation as to the second issue, whether you can discuss about the substance of his testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think that's something that's, by the decisions of both the Appeals Chamber and the Prlic order -- subsequent order, is left to the discretion of the counsel and the accused so that there's no restriction to be placed upon the content of the communication, but that issue can go to the credibility of the accused as a witness and can be inquired on during the cross-examination if there's some kind of suggestive nature to the content -- the contact between the lawyer and the client. But both those decisions have pretty much said that it's best left to the discretion of the counsel as to what kind of communications he would have during the testimony with his client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Leaving it to the parties or the counsel and the accused, the decisions, I take it, presumed a propriety or appropriateness of the contact between the counsel and the accused. So what is appropriate and what is inappropriate, in your observation in terms of substance of the dialogue between the two?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think, Mr. President, that we can look to the concurring opinion of Judges Shahabuddeen and Vaz. In the Appeals Chamber decision they said that counsel is not permitted to advise an accused how he should reply to a question or line of questioning, and I certainly agree with that. Other than that, I think it would have to be on a case-by-case basis. Definitely, Dr. Karadzic is not the kind of individual who has anybody put words in his mouth and I don't see any reason whatsoever that I would be suggesting to him something that he should say. But beyond that, there's a -- I don't think there's any basis for any further restriction -- for any restrictions on the content of our communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. To the extent it is suggested here that the jurisprudence gives rise to a presumed deviation from the normal practice with the witness, we would disagree. As Mr. Robinson has acknowledged, the accused is self-represented. The cases that Mr. Robinson has cited and the cases that we have found are grounded on the right to counsel, that is, on the right that someone who has counsel may possess under those circumstances. So it does not appear that that issue arises here and that, therefore -- and those cases, therefore, should have any impact on the Court's exercise of its discretion in connection with ensuring the integrity of the evidence that's elicited in this case. In addition, we would note that even in a case where the accused was represented, in the Popovic case the Court there decided - and that was in January of 2009, on the 26th of January, 2009 - that an appropriate balance was struck between the right to be represented and the need to safe-guard the integrity of the proceedings by ordering that any contact during cross-examination or re-direct could not involve a discussion of the substance of the testimony. And I emphasise again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was with respect to Pandurevic, Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct. I would emphasise again that that was an appropriate balance in a case where the accused was represented by counsel, which is not a situation we have here. So the balance could be struck otherwise. So in our view, Mr. President, the proper way to proceed would be that contact, per se, would not be prohibited for purposes of issues related to logistical matters or specific legal questions of the type Mr. Robinson has dealt with throughout the course of the case, but in keeping with our practice, there should not be discussion about the substance of the testimony. I would also note one final thing that Mr. Robinson mentioned. The potential cross-examination of the discussion as a remedy for or a way of addressing the possibility of deviations from the expected practice, but of course that gives rise to the further question of the attorney/client privilege and whether or not the invocation of any alleged right to consult with the accused on the substance of the testimony, therefore, is a waiver by citing those cases of the attorney/client privilege. So that would be something the Court would have to consider in such a circumstance; however, as noted, I -- we don't believe it arises here, given that Mr. Karadzic is self-represented and the proper balance should be struck simply by precluding discussion about the substance of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I? May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll come to you. The fact that the accused himself is a self-represented accused, i.e., he's, in other words, lead counsel himself make any difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In our submission, yes, there is a distinction. In previous cases, the Court has had to consider the full range of the right to counsel and its extent, its reach. Now, I don't particularly share the view that stepping into the witness-stand is a stage of the proceedings within the meaning of the term normally used, but that's a different matter. That doesn't arise here. That -- the balance that the courts have attempted to strike in those cases between the scope of the right of representation and the tension between the position of a witness and the need to ensure the integrity of the proceedings only arises when someone is represented by counsel. The -- taking the position of a self-represented accused means, as the -- as this Court pointed out in its earlier decisions, for example, related to the appointment of Mr. Harvey, that the accused has voluntarily undertaken those responsibilities and taken on any obstacles, difficulties, that may arise therefrom. So this is, I think, manifestly a different situation which doesn't give rise to the same balance of considerations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In short, you don't hit the trigger point for striking that balance and we're back in a situation that we normally have where someone takes the stand and we implement very standard safe-guards simply by way of ensuring the integrity of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While he's giving evidence in chief, can he instruct Mr. Robinson to ask certain questions or not to ask certain questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I haven't considered that specifically, but obviously -- it's obvious that there will be a colloquy of sorts taking place. I'm not sure that arises as a particular impediment in the course of communication at that point, but I think -- in other words, whether or not technically it arises as a problem, I don't think from a practical point of view it does. I think there's a communication between the question and the answer -- and the witness that will obviate that problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If there should be any restrictions, that restriction should apply equally to the other members of the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, that's certainly the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, we have only five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Excellency --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm talking about the tape.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe that I will finish within. I believe that over these 500 days we maintained the integrity of the proceedings. On my part, I did my best for that to be the cases. I am sorry I didn't manage to speak to Mr. Robinson about my dilemmas and quandaries, but now I fully understand. I can communicate to you that we are going to save time. I have decided not to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's the end of the story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just in case, we'll have a break. We'll come back to the courtroom at 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And before I forget, we will be filing something, Mr. President. It's relatively imminent, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.58 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Robinson, will the Croatian witness be the last witness for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Depending on the rulings of the Chamber and some pending motions, that seems to be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Pending motions being the motions related to the various intercepts?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was also thinking of the Rule 92 bis motions as well as -- it seems like there's one other motion that may impact upon a witness but it escapes me at the moment, but primarily Rule 92 bis motions. The other one is the sentencing issues, whether we have to call any witnesses on sentencing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the date for the testimony of that Croatian witness remains the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, as far as we're concerned, I sent it to the Embassy of Croatia and they acknowledged having received our notice, but they haven't given any further indication of the availability of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, a while ago the Chamber set the dead-line for your rebuttal motion as 4th of March, but would there be any possibility the Chamber can receive it any earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll certainly -- I mean, I'll communicate that and we'll do our best. I -- that's not -- for various reasons, that's not something I can assure the Court about now, but we'll obviously take the Court's request on board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have just signed the -- an order regarding the close of Defence case, and I take it that it will be filed very soon, in which the Chamber will -- has dealt with the dead-line for any bar table motions and MFI'd documents, et cetera. When this will be done, it will regard the date as the end of Defence case. One thing further I wanted to inquire of the parties is the -- how much time they would need for the final brief? Any observation, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, except I'm pleased the Court is asking. If I had at hand at the moment a specific figure that was the product of an assessment with the entire team and a legitimate projection of what was required, I would share it right now, but we will do so as quickly as possible. Given -- I think this is a reflection of the Court's acknowledgement of the scope of the case and we appreciate that, we'll try to give you the best indication we can as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence fully subscribes to this same reply given by the Prosecution, so the same goes for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It, of course, would be a joint order. It's not as if the Court would consider a dead-line for one and not the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do the parties have anything to raise? Then the hearing is adjourned until 3rd of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 4.00 on 3rd of March. Hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 3rd day of March, 2013, at 4.00 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.08 p.m.,
